extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemaking officials, e-Rulemaking program managers, and administrative law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies on identifying, processing, and responding to mass, malattributed (fraudulent), and computer-generated public comments in notice-and-comment rulemakings, using legal, policy, and technological measures. Includes definitions, processing recommendations, docketing practices, coordination, training, and transparency measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass comment response / mass comment campaign (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comment response: situations where an agency receives an unusually large number of comments (e.g., hundreds or thousands) relative to its typical docket; generally an order-of-magnitude (e.g., ~10x) increase. Mass comment campaign: a special case in which one or more organizations urges or coordinates the submission of large numbers of identical or nearly identical comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed numeric threshold is prescribed; threshold will vary by agency and rule. Mass comment campaigns have grown with cheaper electronic participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malattributed comments (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments falsely attributed to persons by whom they were not, in fact, submitted (also referred to as fraudulent, fake, or malattributed comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution may involve identities that do not exist, people unaware of the comment, or stolen/compromised addresses; enabled by easy access to large personal data sets and automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated comments (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments whose text is generated by a software algorithm rather than written directly by a human commenter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes crude cut-and-paste automation as well as higher-quality NLP-generated text (e.g., GPT-style outputs). Such comments can be submitted automatically via APIs; they may sometimes add value (e.g., error reports), but also risk large-scale, human-quality automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA notice content requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires notice to include (1) a statement of the time, place, and nature of public rulemaking proceedings; (2) reference to the legal authority under which the rule is proposed; and (3) either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must disclose scientific/technical details underlying proposals so the public has a fair opportunity to react and comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to participate; interested persons
rubrics_metrics.description: After notice, the agency must give 'interested persons' an opportunity to participate by submitting written data, views, or arguments with or without opportunity for oral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Person' is broadly defined (individuals, organizations, etc.); courts read participation rights expansively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to significant comments (judicial standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider the relevant matter presented and respond in the final rule to 'significant' comments—those that, if true, would require a change in the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to significant comments can be grounds for remand under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard; but not all comments require a response (see speculative comment exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative/purely speculative comments need not be answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments that are purely speculative and do not disclose a factual or policy basis require no response from the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recognized limit on the APA responsiveness requirement (common-sense rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption to post all comments to the docket promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should post comments promptly to the rulemaking docket upon receipt if the comment is to be included in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt posting enables external correction (e.g., victims of malattribution to flag misuse) and supports transparency and evaluation of docket materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy articulation for excluding/removing comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency decides to exclude or remove duplicate, malattributed, or computer-generated comments from the docket, it should articulate such a policy in advance or provide a reasoned explanation after excluding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is placement in the docket; exclusion requires an affirmative justification in law or agency policy (examples include prohibitions on threatening language, profanity, anonymous comments, copyrighted material).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: If aware of a malattributed comment, an agency should either retain the comment but remove the malattribution (i.e., render it anonymous) or remove the comment from the docket altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are not obligated to affirmatively search for malattributed comments, but may set policies rejecting comments that violate their rules. Anonymization protects the person whose identity was used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not discard computer-generated comments, although they may segregate and treat them separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-generated comments may be retained but flagged/segregated; agencies should be cautious about wholesale deletion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of comments an agency relies upon
rubrics_metrics.description: Any duplicative, malattributed, or computer-generated comment on which an agency actually relies must be placed and retained in the rulemaking docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may anonymize or flag such comments, but reliance requires docket retention to support reason-giving and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing removal opportunities for persons misattributed
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent practicable, agencies should provide opportunities (including potentially after the comment deadline) for individuals whose names have been attached to comments they did not submit to identify and request removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables victims of identity misuse to remedy malattribution; practical processes should be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification to submitter when comment flagged/removed
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency flags a comment as malattributed or computer-generated or removes such a comment from the docket and the submitter provided electronic contact information, the agency should notify the submitter of the agency's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification supports transparency and allows correction/dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of de-duplication software
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should continue to (or begin to) utilize de-duplication software to identify the unique content in submitted comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De-duplication helps process large volumes of duplicate/near-identical comments; agencies commonly use such tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish policies regarding posting duplicate/near-identical comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should publish policies balancing user-friendliness, transparency, and informational completeness about how duplicate and near-identical comments will be posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: posting a single representative example with a count of duplicates and an option to view all, breaking out non-identical content, and providing enhanced search options based on unique information content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider using bulk submission, identity validation, and reCAPTCHA at submission stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies (those using Regulations.gov and those that do not) should consider utilizing bulk submission APIs, identity validation features, reCAPTCHA, or similar tools in their comment submission processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations.gov includes an API for bulk submission, an identity validation feature for authorized bulk submitters, and reCAPTCHA to screen out non-human commenters. These tools may reduce fraudulent/automated submissions but are not perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay abreast of developments in submission and detection technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should monitor evolving technologies related to the submission of mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments so responses can be implemented as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both submission-stage tools and processing-stage detection technologies; ongoing monitoring is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage and adopt technologies for identifying malattributed and computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and relevant coordinating bodies should encourage and stay abreast of technologies for identifying malattributed and computer-generated comments in the docket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investment in and adoption of detection tools can help segregate, flag, or otherwise manage suspicious submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation/flagging of suspicious comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may segregate or flag comments identified as malattributed or computer-generated for separate treatment in analysis and docket presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segregation facilitates transparent handling without necessarily removing comments from the public record, and supports clearer use of reliable inputs in substantive decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies free to set reasonable commenting policies and reject violative comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are free to set reasonable policies concerning the public comment process and to reject comments that violate those policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include late comments or submissions containing prohibited content; however agencies are not required to search proactively for violative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should provide materials explaining what information is useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should consider providing materials (videos, FAQs, etc.) that explain to prospective commenters what information is useful in a public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear guidance in multiple formats can improve comment quality and focus public input on matters useful to rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask specific questions and identify useful information in NPRMs/NOIs/ANPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: In notices (NPRMs, NOIs, ANPRs), agencies should ask specific questions and identify particular information that would be useful in developing the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted questions help elicit substantive, actionable comments rather than generic form submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State whether malattributed/computer-generated comments were removed in final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing a final rule, agencies should state whether they removed from the docket any malattributed and/or computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transparency statement helps explain how questionable inputs were handled and supports public and judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination: share best practices and innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and coordinating bodies should share best practices and relevant innovations for addressing mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments and supplemental participation technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination can accelerate adoption of effective approaches across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination: develop technologies with private sector experts and vendors
rubrics_metrics.description: The e-Rulemaking Program and other coordinating bodies should work with agencies and private sector experts/vendors to develop technologies responding to common issues with mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-private collaboration can produce shared tools and expertise for detection, deduplication, and improved participation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: e-Rulemaking Program should provide a common de-duplication platform
rubrics_metrics.description: The e-Rulemaking Program should provide a common de-duplication platform for agencies to use, though agencies should be free to modify or use another platform as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A shared platform offers economies of scale while allowing agency-specific customization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and staff development
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should offer ongoing training and staff development to respond to the rapidly evolving technologies related to mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments and supplemental participation processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training helps agency staff recognize new threats/opportunities and use available tools effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider supplemental public participation processes enabled by technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should stay abreast of technologies that can facilitate public participation outside the notice-and-comment process (e.g., collaborative annotation, mini-publics, citizen juries, wiki-surveys) and consider using supplemental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental processes can increase meaningful, representative, and expert participation and mitigate problems arising from mass or automated comment campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance user-friendliness, transparency, and informational completeness in docket presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing how comments are posted/presented, agencies should balance values such as user-friendliness, transparency, and informational completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (single representative example plus count, view-all option, breakout of unique content, search by unique content) should reflect tradeoffs among accessibility and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may take affirmative steps to identify malattributed/computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider taking affirmative steps to identify comments that are malattributed or computer-generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not strictly required by law, proactive identification can reduce harms and improve docket quality; methods may include algorithmic detection, manual review, and cross-referencing contact information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat technology-enabled comments as a systemic crisis but take mitigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass, malattributed, and computer-generated comments currently do not fundamentally undermine notice-and-comment rulemaking, but they raise issues warranting mitigation through low- and high-tech measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt practical steps that reduce cost and negative impacts while preserving inclusiveness; employ technology both to manage problematic comments and to enable improved public engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should post comments promptly to enable external correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt posting of comments supports public correction of malattributed comments (e.g., victims noticing misuse) and facilitates transparent evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying posting may prevent detection and correction of wrongful submissions; promptness aids oversight and remediation.
